text: Somebody inside the company is leaking documents, and every day you don't catch them the company loses value. You're the head of security. You can hand out marked copies of a document, a canary trap, and watch which copy leaks. Accuse the right person and you keep what's left. Accuse the wrong one and you lose everything.

Canary is a reinforcement-learning environment for agents. The agent gets thirteen tools: staff lists, documents, access logs, interviews, and canary traps. The score is the company's value at the accusation if it's right, minus one if it's wrong, and zero if it never accuses. So guessing has negative expected value, and so does waiting forever.

A Bayesian reference solver sets the bar. One command, make reproduce, replays the whole table with no API keys. On the hard tier the solver keeps about half the company's value. The obvious shortcuts lose money: reading the logs alone, guessing on day one, or acting at random all score below zero.

Then we gave the same task to Gemini 4 Carbon in the judges' own harness, OpenCode over MCP, on thirty hard worlds paired with the solver. It kept sixty-five percent of the solver's value, and the confidence interval stays below parity. It was right less often, and it accused about two and a half days later on average. We report the parity results too: on medium, and in our own in-process loop, Gemini matches the solver.

Here's one hard world, played by both. The solver spends its first four days planting canaries. By day five the leaks have named the mole, and it accuses. Gemini spends those same days interviewing people: twenty-nine interviews and two canaries. Interviews are weak evidence, and the rules say so. It finds the same person, eleven days later, and by then the company has lost almost half of what the solver saved.

On another world Gemini is fooled. The hard tier tells the agent that one canary readout in twenty points at the wrong copy. Gemini planted its first canary on day four and relied on a single late readout. That readout was wrong, and Gemini called its suspect, quote, uniquely identified. It was the wrong person. The solver had planted eleven canaries by day six, so no single readout could mislead it.

Gemini also reads every trajectory we have in one long context and names the failure modes, with quotes that are checked word for word in code. The biggest one, across every agent family, is accusing before the evidence is in: sixty-one percent of all lost value.

A benchmark is only worth something if you can't game it. We logged every attack we tried on our own reward, forty-three of them, each with a fix and a regression test. A Harbor agent that accuses everyone scores minus one on every trial. Then we let Gemini attack it: fifty-three attackers, most of them reading the entire codebase. Zero verified exploits. To prove the detector works, we reopened one old hole on purpose, and four out of four attackers found it.

Gemini plays the game, explains the failures and attacks the reward, and every Gemini number replays offline without a key. Now it's your turn. The game runs the real environment in your browser, and when the case closes it shows you how the solver did on the same world. Can you beat it?
